141.title: The canopy and the whisk
141.hook: the Granth sits under a canopy while an attendant waves a whisk over it, as for royalty
141.howItsDone: While the Guru Granth Sahib is open, a Sikh sits in attendance and waves the chaur over it; the Granth rests on a raised palki under a canopy, wrapped in rumalas, and is ceremonially opened each morning and closed each night.

segments.voice: Yesterday, matha tekna, the forehead resting before the Guru's word. Your line was bow to the word. Today, a closer look at the front of the room.

Old paintings of Indian courts often show the same scene. A king on a raised throne. Above him, a decorated canopy. Beside him, a servant waving a long, white, feathery whisk, slowly, back and forth, keeping the air moving and the flies away. A picture of royalty. Now walk into a gurdwara and look at the front of the hall. A raised throne. A decorated canopy. Someone sitting behind it, waving a long white whisk, slowly, back and forth. Only there's no king. There's a book.
screen: `A KING ON A RAISED THRONE.` → `A CANOPY, A WAVING WHISK.` → `NO KING. A BOOK.`

segments.voice: The whisk is the chaur, or chaur sahib: long white hair, traditionally from a yak's tail or a horse's, set in a handle often of silver or wood. In old India, waving a chaur over someone was a mark of sovereignty, done for kings and emperors. Sikhs do it for the Guru Granth Sahib, because the Granth is their Guru, and in Sikh understanding the Guru is the true sovereign. Look at the rest of the front. The Granth rests on a small raised platform, the manji sahib, inside a decorated seat or throne, the palki. Above it hangs a canopy, the chanani. The book is wrapped in rumalas, beautiful cloths, often embroidered, which families offer as gifts. Whenever the Granth is open, someone sits in attendance behind it, the granthi or another Sikh, and waves the chaur over it. At night, in many gurdwaras, the Granth is closed with prayers and carried to its own resting room. In the morning it's brought out and opened again: prakash, the light, or the appearance. To an outsider, all this can look like worshipping an object. Sikhs would say it's the opposite. These are the honors an Indian court gave its king, given instead to the word, the teaching, the Guru's voice. The chaur says the most royal thing in the room isn't a person with power. It's the word that tells everyone in the room, rich or poor, they're equal before God.
screen: `CHAUR — A WHISK FOR SOVEREIGNS.` · `THE PALKI, CHANANI, RUMALAS.` · `CLOSED AT NIGHT, OPENED AT DAWN.` · `A COURT'S HONORS, FOR THE WORD.` · then, large: `THE WORD IS HONORED.`

segments.voice: Pick up a book that matters to you, a family Bible, a book of poems, a letter, an old photo album, or just picture one: how do you hold it, where does it live, do you put things on top of it, would you drop it on the floor? Hold it with both hands for a moment. Feel the difference between carrying a thing and honoring it.
Chaur. The whisk waved over the Guru Granth Sahib, the old sign of royalty, given to the word.
Your line: the word is honored. The whisk still moves, slowly, back and forth. See you tomorrow.

142.title: Karah prashad
142.hook: a warm sweet of flour, butter and sugar is given to everyone into cupped hands
142.howItsDone: After Ardas, karah prashad, a sweet of equal parts flour, ghee and sugar made while reciting Gurbani, is touched with a kirpan and served to everyone present alike into cupped hands.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the chaur, the whisk of royalty waved over the Guru. Your line was the word is honored. Today, something you can taste.

Near the end of the service, the prayer called Ardas is said, everyone standing. Then a small stir. Someone comes along the rows with a large steel bowl, and everyone around you holds out two hands, cupped together, like a little bowl of their own. Into your hands goes a warm, soft, glossy lump of something golden. It smells of toasted flour and butter. It's sweet, and still warm. What is it, and why does everyone get exactly the same?
screen: `ARDAS, EVERYONE STANDING.` → `A STEEL BOWL ALONG THE ROWS.` → `SOMETHING WARM IN CUPPED HANDS.`

segments.voice: It's karah prashad. Karah is the large iron pan it's cooked in. Prashad means a gift, grace, something blessed and given. It's equal parts whole wheat flour, ghee, which is clarified butter, and sugar, with water. The flour is roasted in the ghee until golden, the sugar syrup goes in, and it's stirred until thick and shining. The Sikh code of conduct asks that whoever makes it keep clean and recite Gurbani, the Guru's words, while it cooks. So the sweet is made with prayer in it. In the service it's placed before the Guru Granth Sahib. After the Ardas, a Sikh touches it with a kirpan, a small sword, as a sign of acceptance, and then it's shared out. Here's the point: everyone gets it. The Sikh in the front row, the visitor at the back, the rich donor, the person who wandered in off the street. In the Gurus' Punjab, caste rules often kept people from eating from the same dish. Sikhs understand karah prashad, like the langar, as setting that aside on purpose. Same bowl, same sweet, same portion, into everyone's hands. Equality you can taste. A few practical things. You receive it with both hands cupped and eat it there, often wiping your hands on a small tissue after. It's rich, so if you only want a little, quietly say thora, meaning a little, and the server will give you less. Declining it altogether is considered impolite, so asking for a small amount is better.
screen: `KARAH — THE PAN. PRASHAD — A GIFT.` · `FLOUR, GHEE, SUGAR, EQUAL PARTS.` · `EVERYONE GETS THE SAME.` · `EQUALITY YOU CAN TASTE.` · then, large: `SWEET, SHARED, EQUAL.`

segments.voice: If you have something sweet nearby, a piece of fruit, a square of chocolate, a spoon of honey, hold it in your cupped hands; if not, just cup your empty hands in your lap and look at the bowl they make. Think of everyone in the world receiving something today, all given the same amount as you. Then, if you have it, eat it slowly, as a gift.
Karah prashad. The warm sweet of flour, ghee and sugar, given to everyone alike, into cupped hands.
Your line: sweet, shared, equal. Two cupped hands, and no one gets more. Day one hundred forty-two, done.

143.title: The order of the day
143.hook: the day's verse is read from wherever the Granth falls open at the morning service
143.howItsDone: Each morning the Guru Granth Sahib is opened at random and the hymn at the top of the left-hand page is read as the day's hukamnama; the Harmandir Sahib's daily hukamnama is shared online for Sikhs everywhere.

segments.voice: Yesterday, karah prashad, warm in cupped hands. Your line was sweet, shared, equal. Today, back to the morning, and a moment of surprise.

Before dawn in Amritsar, once the Guru Granth Sahib has been brought into the Harmandir Sahib, the granthi opens the great book. Not at a bookmark or a chosen page, but wherever it falls open, and reads. Whatever hymn comes up is the Guru's word for that day, and it travels far beyond Amritsar. Not a horoscope. Not a motivational quote on a poster. A word for the day with weight to it, and chosen by no one.
screen: `BEFORE DAWN IN AMRITSAR.` → `WHEREVER IT FALLS OPEN.` → `CHOSEN BY NO ONE.`

segments.voice: It's called the hukamnama. Hukam means command, order, the Divine Will: you met it in Japji, walk in the hukam. Nama means a letter, a written message. So a hukamnama is a letter of command, a message from the Guru. The Sikh code of conduct describes how it's taken. When the Guru Granth Sahib is opened in the morning, the granthi opens it at random and reads the hymn at the top of the left-hand page, or, if that hymn began on the page before, goes back to its start. That hymn is the day's hukamnama, sometimes simply called the vak, the word. It's often written up on a board so people can read it through the day. Here's what's lovely: nobody chooses it. Not the granthi, not a committee, not you. Sikhs understand it as the Guru speaking to the sangat that day, and some take a line from it as their thought for the day. The daily hukamnama from the Harmandir Sahib is shared around the world, online and on screens in gurdwaras from Birmingham to Vancouver, so Sikhs everywhere can start from the same word. It's taken at other moments too: at a wedding, at a child's naming, before a big decision. A family may ask for one, and the first letter of the hymn often gives the new baby's name its first letter. The word has a history outside the morning, too. The Gurus sent written hukamnamas as letters to distant sangats, and the Akal Takht still issues formal hukamnamas to the whole Sikh community. Day to day, though, it's met here: a book falling open, and a word for today.
screen: `HUKAM — COMMAND. NAMA — A LETTER.` · `THE TOP OF THE LEFT-HAND PAGE.` · `NOBODY CHOOSES IT.` · `SHARED FROM AMRITSAR TO EVERYWHERE.` · then, large: `TODAY'S WORD.`

segments.voice: If you can, look up today's hukamnama from the Harmandir Sahib online; most sites give it in Gurmukhi with an English explanation, so read slowly and look for one line that seems to be speaking to you. If you'd rather not look it up now, sit, ask yourself what you'd hope the day's one word for you would say, and listen to the quiet.
Hukamnama. A letter of command: the hymn read from wherever the Guru Granth Sahib falls open in the morning, the Guru's word for the day.
Your line: today's word. A book falls open, and the day has its hymn. See you tomorrow.

144.title: Sitting in the sangat
144.hook: you can stay for kirtan, eat langar, and leave quietly whenever you wish
144.howItsDone: Sikhs and visitors sit together on the floor for kirtan, katha, Ardas and the hukamnama, coming and going as they need, and then eat together in the langar, sitting side by side in rows.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hukamnama, the Guru's word for the day. Your line was today's word. Today, the gurdwara visit comes to an end, and you stay a while.

Karah prashad is warm in your hands. You came in past the flag: shoes off, head covered, hands washed. You walked up the aisle and bowed, or sat quietly at the back, and watched the whisk moving over the Guru. Now what? Do you have to stay for the whole thing? Can you leave in the middle? And where is everybody going afterward? They're all heading somewhere, and it smells wonderful.
screen: `PRASHAD IN YOUR HANDS.` → `THE FLAG, THE SHOES, THE BOW.` → `NOW WHAT?`

segments.voice: Sangat means company, the gathering, the congregation. Sikhs believe there's something special about sitting together in the Guru's presence, and the Gurus praise the sadh sangat, the company of the holy, again and again. You don't have to know anything to be part of it. You just sit. Mostly you'll hear kirtan: hymns from the Guru Granth Sahib sung to music by ragis, musicians, usually with harmonium and tabla. Sometimes there's katha, a talk explaining a hymn. Then Ardas, the standing prayer, the day's hukamnama, and karah prashad. People come and go through all of it. Nobody takes attendance. You can sit for ten minutes or three hours, and leave quietly whenever you wish, after a small bow if you like. And that smell? It's the langar, the free community kitchen, open to everyone. You sit on the floor in rows, called pangat, side by side with whoever's next to you, and volunteers come along with dal, vegetables, rotis, rice, sometimes kheer. It's vegetarian, so everyone can eat it. Sikh tradition tells that Guru Amar Das asked every visitor to eat in the langar before meeting him, and one story says even the emperor Akbar sat on the floor with everyone else. Rich and poor, Sikh and stranger, same row, same food. Hold out your hands for a roti, and eat as much as you need. Being fed, without being asked a single question: that's the langar.
screen: `SANGAT — THE GATHERING.` · `KIRTAN, KATHA, ARDAS.` · `COME AND GO, NO ATTENDANCE.` · `PANGAT — SIDE BY SIDE IN ROWS.` · then, large: `SIT, EAT, GO IN PEACE.`

segments.voice: Plan a visit, not necessarily for today: think of the gurdwara you found a few days ago, and pick a day when the sangat gathers, perhaps a weekend. Picture the whole of it, the flag, the shoes, the scarf, the hall, the music, the prashad, the langar rows, and yourself sitting as long as feels right, then leaving in peace. If a visit isn't possible for you, picture sitting with people you love at a shared meal.
Sangat. The gathering, the congregation: staying for kirtan, eating in the langar, and leaving quietly whenever you wish.
Your line: sit, eat, go in peace. Tomorrow, a step into the Sikh year. That's day one hundred forty-four.

145.title: Vaisakhi: the harvest
145.hook: a spring harvest day in Punjab that became the birthday of the Khalsa in 1699
145.howItsDone: Sikhs celebrate Vaisakhi, usually on April 13 or 14, with services at the gurdwara, an akhand path, amrit ceremonies, the renewal of the Nishan Sahib, nagar kirtan processions and langar, alongside Punjab's harvest festivities.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sangat, and the langar rows. Your line was sit, eat, go in peace. Today a new stretch begins: the Sikh year.

In Punjab, in April, the wheat turns gold. For months the fields have been green, and then, almost at once, they're the color of bread. Farmers who've watched the sky all winter can finally breathe: the crop is in. So, for centuries, there's been a festival: drums, bhangra dancing in the fields, fairs, new clothes, sweets. Punjabis of every faith celebrate it. But for Sikhs, this harvest day holds something else too. On one Vaisakhi, more than three hundred years ago, something was born.
screen: `THE WHEAT TURNS GOLD.` → `DRUMS, BHANGRA, FAIRS.` → `ONE VAISAKHI, SOMETHING BORN.`

segments.voice: Vaisakhi is the first day of Vaisakh, a month in the Indian solar calendar, and it usually falls on the thirteenth or fourteenth of April. In Punjab it's been the harvest day for a very long time: the spring wheat is ready, the sickles come out, the villages celebrate. The Gurus used this gathering. Guru Amar Das asked Sikhs to come to him at Vaisakhi, and it became a day when the scattered sangat met. Then, in 1699, at Anandpur, Guru Gobind Singh used that same gathering for the call you heard back on day eighty-four: the five beloved, the amrit, the birth of the Khalsa. No retelling today. Just notice where it landed: on a harvest day. And the harvest is a picture the Gurus had used all along. Guru Nanak spent his last years farming at Kartarpur, and in one of his hymns he turns a whole farmer's year inward. In paraphrase: make your mind the plowman and good deeds the farming, let effort be the water and your body the field. Sow the Name as the seed, level the ground with contentment, and keep humility as the fence around it. Then, by grace, the crop comes up. So the Khalsa can be heard as a harvest: two centuries of the Gurus' patient sowing, since Guru Nanak, coming in all at once. And a harvest is also a beginning, because next year's seed comes out of it. That's why Sikhs celebrate both together: harvest and birth. Wherever Sikhs live now, Vaisakhi is one of the biggest days of the year.
screen: `THE FIRST OF VAISAKH, MID-APRIL.` · `THE SANGAT GATHERS AT HARVEST.` · `THE MIND AS PLOWMAN, THE NAME AS SEED.` · `THE END OF GROWING, A NEW SEED.` · then, large: `HARVEST AND BIRTH.`

segments.voice: If you can, look out of a window or step outside, and find something growing or resting, whatever the season where you are: a tree, a weed in the sidewalk, a plant on a shelf, even the grass. Look at it for a moment. Then turn inward: what's been growing slowly in your own life, is any of it ready, and what might be starting right at the end of something?
Vaisakhi. The spring harvest day in Punjab, in mid-April, which in 1699 became the birthday of the Khalsa.
Your line: harvest and birth. The end of growing, and a new seed. See you at the procession.

146.title: Vaisakhi: the procession
146.hook: the Granth is carried through the streets, led by five Sikhs in saffron
146.howItsDone: At Vaisakhi and on gurpurabs, Sikhs hold nagar kirtans: the Guru Granth Sahib is carried through the streets on a decorated float, led by five Sikhs representing the Panj Pyare, with the sangat singing and free food offered along the route.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vaisakhi, the harvest day that became the Khalsa's birthday. Your line was harvest and birth. Today, the same festival, out on the street.

It's a spring morning in a city far from Punjab. A main road has been closed. People are sweeping it, and some are washing it down, though it's already clean. Then you hear it coming: drums, and singing, a whole street of voices. Five figures walk at the front in saffron robes and turbans, swords held upright. Behind them rolls a float covered in flowers, and on it, under a canopy, someone waving a whisk over a book. Behind that, a river of people, singing. The kirtan has left the building.
screen: `A ROAD SWEPT AND WASHED.` → `FIVE IN SAFFRON, SWORDS UPRIGHT.` → `THE KIRTAN LEAVES THE BUILDING.`

segments.voice: It's called a nagar kirtan. Nagar means town; kirtan, you know, is singing the Guru's hymns. So: kirtan through the town. Many are held around Vaisakhi, and others on gurpurabs, the Gurus' anniversaries, through the year. Everything you learned at the gurdwara is here, just outdoors. The Guru Granth Sahib rides in a palki on a decorated float, under a canopy, with someone in attendance waving the chaur. At the front walk five Sikhs representing the Panj Pyare, the beloved five of 1699, in saffron or blue, often barefoot, carrying swords. Often the Nishan Sahib is carried too. Ahead of them all, volunteers sweep and wash the road, as you'd prepare a path for royalty. Behind comes the sangat, singing. Along the way you'll often see gatka, the Sikh martial art, performed with sticks and swords. And all along the route, families set up stalls handing out free food and drinks to anyone passing: samosas, pakoras, sweets, water, tea. It's langar, moved onto the sidewalk. In cities in Canada, the United States and Britain, a nagar kirtan can fill whole streets, and plenty of the people eating along the route aren't Sikh at all. Why take the Guru into the street? Partly celebration. Partly to share: the gurdwara's doors are always open, but here the gurdwara walks out to meet people. And partly as a reminder that the Guru's word isn't meant to stay indoors. It's meant for the whole town.
screen: `NAGAR — TOWN. KIRTAN — SINGING.` · `FIVE IN FRONT, THE GRANTH BEHIND.` · `THE ROAD SWEPT, THE FOOD FREE.` · `THE GURDWARA WALKS OUTSIDE.` · then, large: `THE SONG WALKS OUTSIDE.`

segments.voice: If you can, find a nagar kirtan video and watch a minute of it: the five at the front, the float, the singing crowd. Or, if you'd rather stay quiet, close your eyes and picture a street you know well swept clean, a song coming down it, and food handed out free on every corner. Who would you want to feed?
Nagar kirtan. Singing through the town: the Guru Granth Sahib carried in procession, led by five Sikhs in saffron, with food for everyone along the way.
Your line: the song walks outside. Drums first, then the five, then everyone. Day one hundred forty-six, done.

147.title: Guru Nanak's gurpurab
147.hook: the full moon of Katak marks his birth, with lamps, kirtan and langar
147.howItsDone: Sikhs celebrate Guru Nanak's gurpurab on the full moon of Katak with an akhand path, early-morning prabhat pheris, a nagar kirtan, a full day of kirtan, lamps and langar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nagar kirtan. Your line was the song walks outside. This week: the chaur, karah prashad, the hukamnama, the sangat, Vaisakhi, the procession. Today, a birthday the whole Sikh year looks toward.
screen: `CHAUR · PRASHAD · HUKAMNAMA · SANGAT · VAISAKHI · NAGAR KIRTAN.`

segments.voice: Late autumn, the nights drawing in. In the days before a particular full moon, if you're up very early in a Sikh neighborhood, you might hear singing in the dark streets: small groups walking house to house at dawn, singing hymns. On the day itself, gurdwaras fill from morning to midnight. Lamps line the windows and rooftops. Fireworks go up. And the langar kitchens cook for anyone who comes. It's the birthday of the one who started it all: Guru Nanak.
screen: `SINGING IN THE DARK STREETS.` → `GURDWARAS FULL TILL MIDNIGHT.` → `THE BIRTHDAY OF GURU NANAK.`

segments.voice: A gurpurab is a Guru's day: purab means a festival or holy day, so it's the Guru's festival. Sikhs keep gurpurabs for the Gurus' births, their martyrdoms, and other great moments. Guru Nanak's is sometimes called Prakash Purab, the festival of the light's appearing. It falls on the full moon of Katak, a month in the Indian calendar, usually in November. The celebration builds for days. An akhand path, an unbroken reading of the whole Guru Granth Sahib, is often timed to finish on the morning of the gurpurab. Before it, early-morning processions called prabhat pheris go singing through the streets, and there's often a nagar kirtan. On the day, kirtan and talks about Guru Nanak's life run all day, lamps are lit, and langar feeds everyone. At Nankana Sahib, in Pakistan, where he was born in 1469, pilgrims gather from across the world. Here's an honest detail: the sources don't agree on the month of his birth. Some of the early janamsakhis, the life stories, place it in the spring month of Vaisakh, and some historians follow them. The Bala janamsakhi gives the full moon of Katak, and that's the date the Sikh community celebrates. Sikhs have discussed this at length, and the celebration in Katak remains. What nobody disputes is what the day is for. Bhai Gurdas, in his first Var, says that when the true Guru Nanak appeared, the mist cleared and light spread through the world. The lamps say it without words. And Sikhs say that light didn't go out: it passed through the ten Gurus and rests now in the Granth.
screen: `GURPURAB — THE GURU'S FESTIVAL.` · `THE FULL MOON OF KATAK.` · `PRABHAT PHERIS, LAMPS, LANGAR.` · `THE SOURCES DIFFER ON THE MONTH.` · then, large: `THE LIGHT THAT CAME.`

segments.voice: If you can safely, light a candle or a small lamp, or switch on one soft light and turn off the others, and let the flame be the only thing you watch. Think of one thing you've learned from Guru Nanak on this path: one God, honest work, sharing, the Name remembered, everyone equal at one table. If you pray, you can give thanks; if not, simply honor the light.
Gurpurab. A Guru's festival day. Guru Nanak's, on the full moon of Katak, is kept with lamps, kirtan and langar.
